children: Two-year and five-year British government bond yields rose to a one-week high on Wednesday after oil prices rose above $100 a barrel for the first time in six weeks, reviving inflation fears that pushed yields to their highest in decades last week.

Two-year gilt yields (GB2YT=RR), which are sensitive to interest expectations reached 4.629% at 0925 GMT, up more than 3 basis points on the day and their highest since September 2 when they hit a five-month high of 4.691%.
Five-year yields (GB5YT=RR) peaked at 4.727%, also up 3 bps and their highest since a week ago when they peaked at a three-year high of 4.785%.

"Higher crude (has) revived concerns that the energy shock could stall disinflation and force central banks to remain restrictive," said Daniela Hathorn, senior markets analyst at brokers Capital.com.

Economists polled by Reuters do not expect the Bank of England to raise rates at next week's meeting or later this year, but financial markets on Wednesday priced in a 70% chance of a hike by November's meeting.

BoE Governor Andrew Bailey told a parliament committee on Tuesday that market pricing reflected the risk of further energy market pressure on inflation but that the BoE itself was not seeking to signal that a rate rise was coming.

Earlier on Tueday, Britain issued 30-year benchmark gilts (GB30YT=RR) which will pay a yield of 5.817%, the country's costliest borrowing since at least 1998, adding to pressure on finance minister John Healey ahead of his debut budget next month.
